title: Students Left Without a Snack
statement:
A school canteen has two kinds of snack, type 0 and type 1. Students stand in a queue; students[i] is the only type the i-th student in line will take. The snacks lie in a pile; snacks[0] is on top. There are as many snacks as students.

Each turn the student at the front looks at the top snack. If it is their type, they take it and leave. Otherwise they go to the back of the queue. This repeats until nobody left in the queue wants the top snack.

Return how many students end up without a snack.

examples.why: Students keep rotating until someone wants the top snack. Every snack gets taken.
The one type-1 student takes the first snack. The second snack is also type 1, and the three remaining students all want type 0, so they are stuck.
Both type-1 students eat, then a third type-1 snack sits on top and jams the line. Comparing type totals (only one snack short) would say 1: the pile order matters.

gen: (r, big) => { const n = big ? 100 : r.int(1, 8); return [r.arr(n, 0, 1), r.arr(n, 0, 1)]; }
hints: Students keep cycling, so their order in the queue does not really matter. What does?
The process only stops when the top snack is a type that nobody left in line wants.

Count how many students want each type. Walk the pile from the top: each snack is taken if its count is above zero. The first snack whose count is zero stops everything, and everyone still waiting is left out.

explain.intuition:
Because unhappy students rotate to the back, the queue eventually shows the top snack to every remaining student. So the top snack is taken if and only if at least one remaining student wants that type. Who exactly takes it does not change anything afterwards: only the counts of each type matter.

That turns the simulation into counting. Keep two counters. Go through the pile from the top and decrement the matching counter. The first time the counter for the top snack is already zero, the line is stuck; the answer is the number of students still waiting.
steps: Count students wanting type 0 and type 1.
Walk the snacks from the top.
If the counter for this snack's type is zero, stop: return the sum of both counters.
Otherwise decrement that counter and continue.
If the pile runs out, everyone was fed: return 0.
pitfalls: Comparing the total counts of each type only. The pile order decides when the line jams, as in the third example.
Simulating the queue without a stop condition. You need to stop once a full rotation passes with no one taking the snack, or the loop never ends.

solutions.title: Simulate the queue
solutions.idea: Rotate students exactly as described. Stop when a whole pass over the queue takes no snack.

solutions.title: Count each type
solutions.idea: Only the number of students per type matters. Walk the pile and stop at the first snack nobody wants.

followups: There are now k snack types instead of two. Does the counting idea still work?
Return which students (by original position) go hungry. Can you still avoid full simulation?
